title: Inversion after negative and restrictive expressions
objectives: Form statements with initial negative and restrictive expressions.
Place inversion in the correct clause.
Contrast emphatic fronting with neutral word order.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Writers sometimes place a negative or restrictive expression at the beginning of a clause to give it emphasis or connect it to the preceding argument. “Rarely have we seen such a result” highlights how unusual the result is. This ordering is more typical of formal writing and prepared speech than of relaxed conversation. The ordinary order, “We have rarely seen such a result”, is also standard.

Inversion means placing an auxiliary verb before the subject. It is similar in form to question order, but the sentence remains a statement. Fronting a negative or restrictive expression can trigger this inversion in the main clause: “Under no circumstances should visitors open the cabinet.”

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: With an existing auxiliary, move it before the subject: “Never have I heard that version” and “Little did they know what would happen.” If a simple present or past clause has no auxiliary, add do, does or did and use the base form: “Seldom do we receive complaints” and “Never did she mention the cost.” With main verb be, put be before the subject: “Rarely is the room empty.”

The restrictive expression must be in the relevant initial position. Compare “Only after the meeting did we understand” with “We understood only after the meeting”. In the first, only after the meeting is fronted and the main clause is inverted. In the second, the expression follows the verb and does not trigger inversion.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: In a safety notice, “At no time may visitors enter the laboratory alone” gives a strong restriction. In a narrative, “Not until the lights went out did they notice the sound” postpones the main clause until after the time clause. The inversion is in “did they notice”, not inside “the lights went out”.

Compare “Only when the report arrived did she call” with “Only she called”. In the second sentence, only modifies the subject she; it does not trigger the pattern taught here. “Not only did she call, but she also wrote” is another main-clause pattern, though writers need not use it whenever they want to add information.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not insert an auxiliary and retain a past-tense main verb: “Never did he say that”, not “Never did he said that”. After did, the main verb is in its base form. Equally, do not invert the subordinate clause in “Only when the rain stopped did we leave”: the inversion belongs in the main clause.

These patterns often sound emphatic or formal. Their absence is not an error, and overusing them can make ordinary prose sound dramatic. In a neutral account, “We rarely receive complaints” is usually simpler; choose the fronted version when its emphasis serves the context.

examples.sentence: Rarely have we seen such a result.
examples.note: Have comes before the subject after initial rarely.

examples.sentence: Never did she mention the cost.
examples.note: Did carries past tense and mention stays in the base form.
Do supplies the auxiliary in the present simple.

examples.sentence: At no time were the documents unattended.
examples.note: Were precedes the subject in this passive clause.

examples.sentence: Only after lunch did the visitors leave.
examples.note: The fronted restrictive phrase triggers inversion.

examples.sentence: Not until the rain stopped did we leave.
examples.note: Inversion occurs in the main clause.
Only modifies the subject and does not trigger this inversion.

examples.sentence: We rarely see a queue here.
examples.note: Without initial rarely, ordinary subject–verb order is natural.

common_errors.incorrect: Never she had seen the report.
common_errors.correct: Never had she seen the report.

common_errors.incorrect: Rarely did he mentioned the problem.
common_errors.correct: Rarely did he mention the problem.
common_errors.reason: Did is followed by the base form.

common_errors.incorrect: Only when did the rain stop we left.
common_errors.correct: Only when the rain stopped did we leave.
common_errors.reason: Invert the main clause after the complete fronted time clause.

summary: Initial negative or restrictive expressions can trigger auxiliary–subject inversion.
Use do, does or did when an appropriate auxiliary is absent.
Place inversion in the main clause and choose the emphasis to suit the register.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct form: Rarely ___ such careful work.
exercises.explanation: Initial rarely is followed by the auxiliary have and the subject we.

option_feedback.a: “we have seen” does not fit here. Initial rarely is followed by the auxiliary have and the subject we.
option_feedback.b: “have we seen” fits here. Initial rarely is followed by the auxiliary have and the subject we.
option_feedback.c: “have seen we” does not fit here. Initial rarely is followed by the auxiliary have and the subject we.
option_feedback.d: “we seen have” does not fit here. Initial rarely is followed by the auxiliary have and the subject we.

exercises.prompt: Complete the past statement: Never ___ the price.
exercises.explanation: Did precedes the subject and mention is the base form.

option_feedback.a: “she did mentioned” does not fit here. Did precedes the subject and mention is the base form.
option_feedback.b: “she mentioned did” does not fit here. Did precedes the subject and mention is the base form.
option_feedback.c: “did she mentioned” does not fit here. Did precedes the subject and mention is the base form.
option_feedback.d: “did she mention” fits here. Did precedes the subject and mention is the base form.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses initial only after?
exercises.explanation: The auxiliary precedes the subject after the complete restrictive phrase.

options.text: Only after lunch did the guests leave.
Only after lunch the guests did left.
Only after did lunch the guests leave.
Only after lunch did leave the guests.

option_feedback.a: “Only after lunch did the guests leave.” fits here. The auxiliary precedes the subject after the complete restrictive phrase.
option_feedback.b: “Only after lunch the guests did left.” does not fit here. The auxiliary precedes the subject after the complete restrictive phrase.
option_feedback.c: “Only after did lunch the guests leave.” does not fit here. The auxiliary precedes the subject after the complete restrictive phrase.
option_feedback.d: “Only after lunch did leave the guests.” does not fit here. The auxiliary precedes the subject after the complete restrictive phrase.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct time-clause pattern.
exercises.explanation: The time clause retains normal order; did we leave is inverted.

options.text: Not until did the rain stop we left.
Not until the rain stopped we did left.
Not until the rain stopped did we leave.
Not until stopped the rain did we leave.

option_feedback.a: “Not until did the rain stop we left.” does not fit here. The time clause retains normal order; did we leave is inverted.
option_feedback.b: “Not until the rain stopped we did left.” does not fit here. The time clause retains normal order; did we leave is inverted.
option_feedback.c: “Not until the rain stopped did we leave.” fits here. The time clause retains normal order; did we leave is inverted.
option_feedback.d: “Not until stopped the rain did we leave.” does not fit here. The time clause retains normal order; did we leave is inverted.

exercises.prompt: Choose the neutral statement without fronting.
exercises.explanation: Without an initial restrictive expression, the subject normally precedes have.

option_feedback.a: “Have rarely we seen this.” does not fit here. Without an initial restrictive expression, the subject normally precedes have.
option_feedback.b: “Rarely we have seen this.” does not fit here. Without an initial restrictive expression, the subject normally precedes have.
option_feedback.c: “Rarely have seen we this.” does not fit here. Without an initial restrictive expression, the subject normally precedes have.
option_feedback.d: “We have rarely seen this.” fits here. Without an initial restrictive expression, the subject normally precedes have.

exercises.prompt: Which expression in “Only she knew” does only modify?
exercises.explanation: Only modifies she here; the sentence does not use initial-adjunct inversion.

option_feedback.a: “The place.” does not fit here. Only modifies she here; the sentence does not use initial-adjunct inversion.
option_feedback.b: “The time of knowing.” does not fit here. Only modifies she here; the sentence does not use initial-adjunct inversion.
option_feedback.c: “The subject she.” fits here. Only modifies she here; the sentence does not use initial-adjunct inversion.
option_feedback.d: “The auxiliary did.” does not fit here. Only modifies she here; the sentence does not use initial-adjunct inversion.
